name: Satan
line: The rebel archangel, once Lucifer, who leads the revolt against God and then sets out to ruin mankind.
about: Satan dominates the opening books, rallying his defeated army in Hell, steering the great council, and crossing Chaos alone to find the new world. Milton gives him the poem’s grandest speeches, full of defiance, wounded pride and self-deception, and then lets him shrink: from a towering commander to a cormorant, a toad, a serpent, and finally a hissing snake among snakes. His soliloquies show a mind that knows it is in torment and cannot repent. Since Blake said Milton was ‘of the Devil’s party without knowing it,’ readers have argued over whether Satan is the poem’s hero or a brilliant study of how evil talks itself into greatness.

name: Beelzebub
line: Satan’s second-in-command, the first to wake beside him on the burning lake.
about: Beelzebub is Satan’s closest ally and the first fallen angel to speak to him in Hell. At the council in Book 2 he rises like ‘a pillar of state’ and puts forward the plan to attack God through his new creation, Man, a plan that the narrator notes was Satan’s all along. Milton draws him as statesmanlike and grave, a ruined dignity rather than a monster. He shows how Satan works through others, letting a lieutenant voice the scheme so the assembly feels it has chosen freely.

name: Moloch
line: The fiercest of the fallen angels, later worshipped with child sacrifice.
about: Moloch heads the catalogue of devils in Book 1, ‘besmeared with blood of human sacrifice,’ the god for whom children were burned in the valley of Hinnom. At the council he speaks first and demands open war, preferring to be destroyed rather than to be less. In the war in Heaven he boasts against Gabriel and is cut in half, fleeing ‘bellowing.’ Milton makes him pure rage without a plan, and readers often take his speech as the simplest of the four positions in the debate.

name: Belial
line: The most graceful and the most idle of the fallen angels, a smooth persuader.
about: Belial has no temples, but Milton says he fills courts, palaces and cities, wherever luxury and violence go together. At the council he argues against war with real eloquence, asking who would give up ‘this intellectual being’ for annihilation, but the narrator warns that he could ‘make the worse appear the better reason.’ In the war in Heaven he trades puns with Satan over the devilish cannon. Readers find him the most modern of the devils, a reasonable voice for doing nothing.

name: Mammon
line: The fallen angel of wealth, who even in Heaven gazed down at the golden pavement.
about: Mammon leads the crew that digs gold out of the hill in Hell to build Pandemonium, and Milton says he first taught men to rifle the earth for treasure. At the council he argues that they should forget Heaven and build a rival empire in Hell, working ‘ease out of pain.’ His speech has a stubborn dignity and an appealing self-reliance, which is exactly its danger. He is Milton’s picture of a mind that measures everything by what it can own and make.

name: Mulciber
line: The architect of Pandemonium, known to the Greeks as Hephaestus and to the Romans as Vulcan.
about: Mulciber appears only briefly in Book 1, as the designer of Satan’s palace, who built towers in Heaven before he fell. Milton retells the myth of Vulcan thrown from Olympus, falling all day ‘from morn to noon … from noon to dewy eve,’ in some of the poem’s most beautiful lines. Then he cuts the myth off: ‘thus they relate, erring.’ The passage is a famous example of Milton using classical stories for their beauty while insisting that his own story is the true one behind them.

name: Sin
line: Satan’s daughter, born from his head, who keeps the gates of Hell.
about: Sin is half a beautiful woman and half a serpent, with hellhounds that creep back into her womb. She tells Satan that she sprang from his head when he first plotted rebellion, that he fell in love with his own image in her, and that their son is Death, who then raped her. She unlocks the gates of Hell for him, and in Book 10 she builds the bridge to the world with Death. The episode is a grotesque parody of the Father and the Son, and readers have long argued about whether such open allegory fits in an epic.

name: Death
line: The son of Satan and Sin, a shapeless, crowned horror who hungers for the world.
about: Death is the poem’s most famous shadow: a shape ‘that shape had none,’ black as Night, carrying a dart and wearing what seems a crown. He nearly fights his own father at Hell’s gate until Sin stops them. In Book 10 he scents the carnage of the fallen world, helps build the bridge, and arrives in Eden hungry to devour everything. Milton’s refusal to give him a clear outline is often praised as the sublime at its best, a horror made out of what the reader cannot picture.

name: Chaos
line: The ancient ruler of the formless abyss between Heaven and Hell.
about: Chaos is both a place, the wild deep of unformed matter, and a person, the ‘Anarch old’ who sits enthroned there with Night. When Satan reaches his court in Book 2, Chaos gives him directions to the new world, glad of anything that will spread disorder. He is a rare morally neutral figure, more aggrieved than evil, resenting how Hell and the created world have eaten into his realm. Scholars debate how far Milton’s Chaos is bad, since God creates the world out of its raw material.

name: God the Father
line: The almighty creator, who foresees the Fall and decrees both justice and mercy.
about: God speaks first in Book 3, looking down on Satan’s flight and explaining that he made men ‘sufficient to have stood, though free to fall.’ Milton gives him the arguments of a theologian: foreknowledge is not compulsion, and justice must be satisfied before mercy can work. He exalts the Son, sends Raphael to warn Adam, and sends Michael to expel him. Many readers, from Alexander Pope to William Empson, have found this God cold or defensive, while others argue that his plain speech is meant to contrast with Satan’s rhetoric.

name: The Son
line: The only Son of God, who offers to die for mankind and later becomes Christ.
about: The Son sits at the Father’s right hand and in Book 3 volunteers to take on human death so that Man can be saved, when no angel will. His exaltation in Book 5 is what provokes Satan’s envy and rebellion. In Book 6 he drives the rebel army out of Heaven alone in his chariot, in Book 7 he creates the world, and in Book 10 he judges Adam and Eve and clothes them. Milton presents him as the perfect obedient son, and readers debate how far the poem reflects Milton’s private belief that the Son is less than the Father.

name: Raphael
line: The ‘sociable spirit’ God sends to warn Adam of his danger.
about: Raphael visits Eden in Book 5, eats lunch with Adam and Eve, and stays the afternoon to tell the story of Satan’s revolt, the war in Heaven and the Creation. He is warm, patient and curious, happy to explain how angels eat and, with a blush, how they love. He also warns Adam, more than once, to be content with what concerns him and not to let passion for Eve override his judgement. Readers have asked whether his long tales really prepare Adam, or whether Milton shows the limits of even the best teaching.

name: Michael
line: The warrior archangel who leads Heaven’s armies and later expels Adam and Eve from Paradise.
about: Michael commands the loyal angels in the war in Heaven and wounds Satan with a sword from God’s armoury. In Books 11 and 12 he comes to Eden as a stern prince to announce the expulsion, then shows Adam visions of history and tells him the rest, through to the Redemption. He is graver than Raphael but deeply humane, teaching temperance, patience and the ‘paradise within.’ Some readers find the last two books a long sermon, while others see Michael’s history lesson as the true preparation for the world outside.

name: Gabriel
line: The chief of the angel guards at the gate of Paradise.
about: Gabriel sits between the rocky pillars of Eden’s gate and sends his angels to search the garden by night after Uriel warns him. When Ithuriel and Zephon bring Satan in, Gabriel confronts him with cool contempt and calls his bluff. The standoff ends when God hangs out golden scales in the sky, and Satan flees. Gabriel also fights in the war in Heaven, where he splits Moloch. He embodies calm, lawful authority set against Satan’s bluster.

name: Uriel
line: The archangel who stands in the sun, regent of its light, and is deceived by Satan.
about: Uriel is one of the seven angels nearest God’s throne, and Satan finds him standing in the sun in Book 3. Disguised as a young cherub, Satan asks the way to the new world, and Uriel, seeing no hypocrisy, points it out with praise for his zeal. Later he notices Satan’s face darken with passion on a mountain and glides down on a sunbeam to warn Gabriel. Milton uses him to show that even a wise angel cannot see through hypocrisy, which only God can detect.

name: Abdiel
line: The one angel in Satan’s camp who stands up to him and walks out alone.
about: Abdiel is a seraph among Satan’s followers when Satan first declares rebellion. He alone protests, arguing that the Son made the angels and that God’s rule is just, and then leaves through the hostile crowd unharmed. In the war in Heaven he strikes the first blow, sending Satan reeling back on his knees. Milton, often isolated himself after the Restoration, praises him as ‘faithful only he,’ and readers see him as the poem’s model of solitary integrity.

name: Ithuriel
line: One of the two angels Gabriel sends to search the garden, whose spear exposes Satan.
about: Ithuriel and Zephon find Satan squatting like a toad at Eve’s ear, whispering dreams into her imagination. Ithuriel touches him lightly with his spear, and because no falsehood can endure the touch of heavenly temper, Satan springs up in his own shape like gunpowder catching a spark. The moment gives the language its phrase ‘Ithuriel’s spear’ for any test that reveals the truth. He appears only in this episode of Book 4.

name: Zephon
line: Ithuriel’s companion, who tells the unmasked Satan how far he has fallen.
about: Zephon searches the garden with Ithuriel in Book 4. When Satan, unmasked, scorns them for not knowing him, Zephon answers ‘scorn with scorn’: Satan’s glory left him when his goodness did. Satan stands abashed and feels ‘how awful goodness is,’ one of the moments where he sees what he has lost. Zephon is young and bold, and his rebuke shows a lesser angel morally stronger than the fallen archangel.

name: Adam
line: The first man, made from the earth to tend Eden and rule over its creatures.
about: Adam is curious, affectionate and eager to learn, questioning Raphael about the stars and telling him about his own first memories and his request for a partner. His love for Eve is the best thing in him and also his weak point; he eats the fruit ‘not deceived, but fondly overcome with female charm.’ After the Fall he despairs, blames Eve, and argues bitterly with God before he repents. Readers argue over whether his choice to die with Eve is the poem’s great act of love or its most fatal error.

name: Eve
line: The first woman, made from Adam’s rib, ‘the mother of all living.’
about: Eve first appears beside Adam in Book 4, recalling how she woke and fell in love with her own reflection in a pool before being led to him. She has an unsettling dream, insists on working alone, and is persuaded by the serpent to eat the fruit. After the Fall, it is her humble plea for forgiveness that reconciles the pair and begins their repentance, and the promise of her seed gives the poem its hope. Feminist readers have argued fiercely over whether Milton’s Eve is subordinated or given more inner life than any other character.

name: The Muse
line: The heavenly voice Milton calls on to inspire his song, named Urania in Book 7.
about: Milton opens Books 1, 3, 7 and 9 with prayers for inspiration, adapting the classical epic’s appeal to the Muse. His Muse is the one who inspired Moses on Sinai, and he also calls on the Spirit that brooded over the abyss at the Creation, and on holy Light. In Book 7 he names her Urania but says he means ‘the meaning, not the name,’ and in Book 9 he says she visits him nightly and dictates his ‘unpremeditated verse.’ These invocations frame the poem as inspired truth rather than invention.

name: The Narrator
line: The blind poet’s own voice, telling the story and breaking in to comment, lament and pray.
about: The narrator sets out to ‘justify the ways of God to men’ and steps forward often: to mourn his blindness at the start of Book 3, to complain of falling on evil days in Book 7, and to grieve over Eve as she leaves Adam’s side. He judges his characters openly, warning that Satan’s fine words are lies. Stanley Fish argued that the narrator deliberately lets readers fall for Satan and then corrects them, so the poem teaches by catching us out.
